# First Contact with Stan {#sec-chap-905} :::::: {#obj-chap-905} ::::: my-objectives ::: my-objectives-header Objectives ::: ::: my-objectives-container This chapter experiments with [RStan: the R interface to Stan](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/vignettes/rstan.html). My aim is to get a better understanding of the underlying functionality of {**RStan**} in connection to the Stan platform. After applying the `rstan::stan()` function several times, especially during working of the Exercises in @sec-006-exercises, I came up with several questions such as: - How to use `.stan` files for applying the Stan modelling language? - What do the MCMC sampling messages mean? - How to minimize execution time for the simulations? This appendix collects my experiments and gives answer to the questions above. I have used as central example functioning as an advanced organizer the code for the Beta-Binomial model in @sec-006-beta-binomial-example. ::: ::::: :::::: ## Introduction ::: {#nte-905-terminology-using-leo .callout-note} ###### Using LLMs for clarification of terminology and procedures The book "Bayes rules!" aims to reduce complexity by honing the process of Bayesian modeling, sampling, and inference to the bare bones. But this reduction in complexity comes at the expense of conceptual clarity and modeling flexibility. The following content is my own summary of conversations with Brave Leo AI. It took me several days to gradually build my understanding of flexible Bayesian understanding. In @sec-chap-006, I had my first contact with the {**rstan**} package. After applying the code snippets guided by the book examples, at least since working on the exercises, I became aware that I did not understand the whole picture: - What is the relationship of {**rstan**} to the [Stan](https://mc-stan.org/), (another?) software for Bayesian Data Analysis? - What are the relationships to other software packages, like {**cmdstanr**} (R Interface to 'CmdStan'), {**rstanarm**} (Bayesian Applied Regression Modeling via Stan), {**brms**} (Bayesian Regression Models using 'Stan'). These questions are not only important conceptually but also practically. It needs a deeper understanding to guide efficient practice: - How to minimize execution time for statistical modeling and sampling? - How do the two steps (defining the model and sampling) work together? - When to use which package? **Naming conventions:** - When I refer in prose to the package names I am going to use capitalization like `RStan` or `CmdStanR.` - When I refer to the package names formally I use {**rstan**} resp. {**cmdstanr**}. - When I use the package names in R code I write `rstan::` or `cmdstanr::` ::: :::::: my-resource :::: my-resource-header ::: {#lem-905-stan-resources} : Used RStan resources ::: :::: ::: my-resource-container - The most authoritative resource is the manual [Stan: Software for Bayesian Data Analysis](https://mc-stan.org/). But I have to confess that many parts I do not understand currently (2026-03-17). - The next session draws therefore from the vignette [RStan: the R interface to Stan](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstan/vignettes/rstan.html), an introduction to using {**RStan**}, the R interface to [Stan](https://mc-stan.org/). Even the majority of the introductory vignette content is still too complex for my understanding. But to get a better understanding for the interaction between RStan and Stan software is exactly the goal of the exerpiments in this annex. - Additionally I have addressed my questions one by one asking LLMs. Many of my questions were about details and adaptions of the modeling procedure covered in [Bayes Rules!](https://www.bayesrulesbook.com/). ::: :::::: ## Different Software for Bayesian Analysis {#sec-905-software-for-bayesian-analysis} ### Stan ≠ R Stan is **not** an R package. It's a separate probabilistic programming language with its own syntax. RStan and CmdStanR are just **interfaces** between R and Stan. When you write a Stan model, you're writing in a language that R cannot execute directly. - **Stan** is the core probabilistic programming language and inference engine that performs Bayesian computation using algorithms like NUTS (No-U-Turn Sampler), optimization (BFGS/L-BFGS), and variational inference (ADVI). - **CmdStan** is the command-line interface to Stan. It doesn’t add new functionality; it’s just a way to execute Stan models without needing R or Python wrappers. It’s how you run Stan programs from the terminal or via other interfaces like - **CmdStanR** is an R package that provides a lightweight interface to Stan calling the command-line interface CmdStan for compilation and running algorithms. It avoids direct C++ integration via {**Rcpp**}. This approach provides benefits like compatibility with the latest Stan versions, fewer installation errors, active maintenance, lower memory overhead, and a more permissive license. It's the appropriate choice for users who want to use the latest Stan features or work with custom Stan models. It’s also ideal for modular workflows where Stan handles computation and downstream R packages (like {**posterior**} or {**bayesplot**}) handle analysis. CmdStanR is currently generally recommended for new projects. - **RStan** is an R package {**rstan**} that provides an in-memory interface relying on R packages like {**Rcpp**} and inline to call C++ code from R. While it offers familiar R syntax, it may lag behind in supporting the latest Stan features due to the complexity of maintaining compatibility with Stan releases. ### Different layers: #### The car analogy Think of the different terms and packages this way: - **Hardware (Processor)** = The actual physical engine that does computation — the CPU executing machine code . - **Operating System** = The mechanic's shop that manages how the engine runs, allocates resources, handles communication between components . - **Stan** = The engine design and fuel (the probabilistic programming language and algorithms like NUTS). - **RStan** = You hire a mechanic (Rcpp) to bolt Stan's engine directly into your R car's chassis. The mechanic must rebuild the engine for your specific shop (OS) and car model (R version). If Stan releases a new engine design, the mechanic must rebuild everything — this takes time and often breaks things . - **CmdStan** = A standalone engine factory that produces ready-made Stan engines. The factory handles all OS and processor details internally. --- Your R car sends a messenger (command-line interface) to the factory, orders a Stan engine run, and the factory delivers results via files. The factory (CmdStan) handles OS/processor compatibility — your R car doesn't need to know the details. #### The place of R in the car analogy Think of the role of R this way: You’re the driver — you tell the car *where to go* (specify the model), and the car’s systems (R + CmdStanR + Stan) handle *how to get there* (computation) without you needing to know engine mechanics. **R (or Python)** = The driver’s cockpit and dashboard — it’s where you sit, steer, and interact with the car. R is your control panel. You don’t need to understand the engine (Stan), the factory (CmdStan), or the mechanic (Rcpp) to drive — you just use the controls (functions like `brms::brm()` or `rstanarm::stan_glm()`). - **R/Python** provides the *user interface* — the commands, data structures, and visualization tools you use to specify models, run analyses, and interpret results. - It’s the *glue* that connects you to the engine (Stan) via interfaces like CmdStanR or RStan. - It handles data preprocessing, model diagnostics, plotting, and integration with tidyverse/tidymodels — all the “applied statistics” work you care about. ### Stan, RStan, CmdStanR and brms #### RStan versus CmdStanR **Stan is the core engine**, and all other packages are interfaces to it. The key difference between **RStan** and **CmdStanR** lies in how they connect to Stan: - **RStan** uses Rcpp to call C++ code directly from R, which can lead to installation issues and compatibility problems with newer Stan versions (see: [CmdStanR: the R interface to CmdStan](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/reference/cmdstanr-package.html)). It may also be slower for some tasks due to overhead in reading output files (see: [Google Groups](https://groups.google.com/g/stan-dev/c/BujPDKpUDp0/m/zmImoHyNacYJ)). - **CmdStanR** calls the command-line interface (CmdStan) instead, avoiding direct C++ integration. This results in fewer installation errors, better compatibility with the latest Stan releases, and a more permissive license (see: [Package {cmdstanr}](https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev/cmdstanr)). CmdStanR is not hosted on CRAN, but available at . However, it may be slower for simple models due to file I/O overhead. But this performance difference (e.g., 1s vs 3s for a simple model) is negligible for my work. My focus is on stability and ease of use rather than micro-optimizations. See also the summary section [Comparison with RStan](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html#comparison-with-rstan) of the vignette "Getting started with CmdStanR. #### Using CmdStanR from the beginning For learning Bayesian statistics, Claude Haiku recommends to **start with cmdstanr from the beginning**: **Easier installation**: {**cmdstanr**} avoids the C++ compiler configuration issues that often plague {**rstan**} setup[^905-rstan-tutorial-1]. This lets you focus on learning statistics rather than troubleshooting installation problems. [^905-rstan-tutorial-1]: Some of the installation complexities is explained in the [FAQ for the Aalto course 2025](https://avehtari.github.io/BDA_course_Aalto/FAQ.html). **Modern design**: {**cmdstanr}** is the newer, actively developed interface. It doesn't directly call C++ from R like {**rstan**} does; instead, it uses CmdStan behind the scenes for compilation and running algorithms[^905-rstan-tutorial-2]. This separation actually makes {**cmdstanr}** more reliable and easier to maintain. [^905-rstan-tutorial-2]: See the vignette: [Getting started with CmdStanR](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanr/articles/cmdstanr.html) **Better for teaching**: {**cmdstanr}** provides a similar user experience across different programming languages. So if you ever learn Stan in other languages, the concepts transfer directly. **Performance advantages**: {**cmdstanr}** supports within-chain multithreading more intelligently and tends to compile models faster with better detection of when recompilation is needed[^905-rstan-tutorial-3]. [^905-rstan-tutorial-3]: See documentation for [parallelization](https://mc-stan.org/docs/cmdstan-guide/parallelization.html). The only reason to learn {**rstan**} first would be if one is working with legacy code or packages that specifically require it. Since I am starting fresh, {**cmdstanr**} is the better choice. ::: {#nte-905-cmdstanr-over-rstan .callout-note} ###### Applying CmdStanR instad of Rstan Brave Leo AI and other sources recommend CmdStanR {**cmdstanr**} over RStan {**rstan**}. Summarized the reasons that matters me most are threefold: - speed, - stability, - and up-to-date integration with Stan. Instead following "Bayes rules!" approach with {**rstan**} I will therefore apply in this text mainly {**cmdstanr**}. ::: #### And what about {**brms**}? The only disadvantage of CmdStanR is that I have to learn Stan syntax. There is the possibility of using {**brms**} as an even higher-level interface on top of CmdStanR and Stan for standard models, without learning Stan syntax. {**brms**} is an R package that provides a flexible interface for fitting **Bayesian generalized (non-)linear multivariate multilevel models** using **Stan**, the most widely used probabilistic programming language for full Bayesian inference. - It supports a wide range of response distributions and link functions, enabling users to fit models for **linear, robust linear, count data, survival, response times, ordinal, zero-inflated, hurdle, and mixture models** within a multilevel framework. - The package uses a formula syntax similar to {**lme4**,} making it accessible to users familiar with frequentist mixed models. - Key features include: - **Distributional regression**: All parameters of the response distribution (e.g., mean, variance, shape) can be modeled as functions of predictors. - **Non-linear and smooth terms**: Supports theory-driven and data-driven non-linear effects. - **Advanced modeling options**: Auto-correlation structures, censoring, truncation, meta-analytic standard errors, missing data imputation, and spatial models (e.g., CAR structures). - **Flexible prior specification**: Encourages the use of informative priors that reflect prior knowledge. - **Model evaluation**: Offers tools for posterior predictive checks, leave-one-out cross-validation (LOO), WAIC, and Bayesian R-squared. The package is actively maintained, with version **2.23.1** as of January 2026, and is available on CRAN and GitHub. {**brms**} is widely used in social sciences, biostatistics, and other fields requiring robust, flexible Bayesian modeling. #### Andvantages of starting with {**brms**} - {**brms**} has the major advantage that I **don't need to learn Stan syntax** at all. The package uses familiar R formula notation (like `y ~ x1 + x2`), making Bayesian modeling accessible without Stan knowledge. - {**brms**} is not "advanced only" — it is actually suited **for beginners and practitioners who want to fit standard Bayesian models quickly**. One can do serious applied work without touching Stan code. One gets Bayesian inference without the Stan learning curve. - {**brms**} original **documentation is excellent** and comprehensive. Additionally there are many other tutorials to learn this package. - With `brms::stancode()` one can **inspect generated Stan code**. Learning through inspection (seeing what {**brms**} generates) is often more efficient than learning Stan syntax from scratch. - Bayesian diagnostics (trace plots, Rhat, effective sample size) work the same way regardless of interface. They catch problems which is another learning possibility to apply {**brms**} correctly. For all these advantages Claude Haiku stated: **Start with {brms}, learn {cmdstanr} only if needed.** **When to learn CmdStanR:** - When {**brms**} can't express your model (e.g., custom likelihood, complex hierarchical structures) - After I have internalized Bayesian thinking through {**brms**} workflows - To deepen conceptual understanding of what's happening "under the hood" #### Looking into brms sporadically In contrast to Claude Haiku’s recommendation, I will start with {**cmdstanr**}. The reason is that I am afraid I will digress too much from the book content on "Bayes rules!" This annex already gives me a headache, because I have to learn everything from scratch. Understanding Bayesian modeling by reading "Bayes rules!" Especially trying to solve the exercises are very helpful in this respect. 2. Translating the book's code into {**cmdstanr**} functions and writing it down as notes following the structure of the book. 3. Looking into {**brms**} and trying to develop the book models with {**brms**} syntax. But my text to this part will perhaps not be complete and I will therefore write these kind of notes separately in annex chapters. ::: {.callout-note #nte-905-future-plans} ###### Future Plans After I have finished "Bayes rules!" [@johnson2022] I plan to foster my understanding of Bayesian analysis with "Statistical Rethinking" [@mcelreath2023] followed by "Bayesian Data Analysis" [@gelman2013]. ::: ## Compilation & MCMC Sampling The function used in the book `rstan::stan()` combines these two process phases into "# STEP 2: SIMULATE the posterior". But using the nomenclature of the book there are actually three steps: ### Defining the model Writing the data, parameters, model, and generated quantities blocks in Stan, a probabilistic programming language with its own syntax (Step 1 in the book). There are two options: Writing a character string as done in the book, or recommended -- especially with complex models -- writing the definition into a file. - Compilation: - Sampling ### Compilation The compilation step translates your Stan model through **multiple layers**: #### Stan -> C++ -> Machine Code 1. **Stan → C++**: The Stan compiler (*stanc*) parses your `.stan` model and translates it into C++ code. This includes: - Parsing the `data`, `parameters`, `model`, and `generated quantities` blocks - Performing **automatic differentiation** setup — Stan needs gradients of your log-posterior for its samplers, so the C++ code is structured to compute these efficiently - Type-checking and validating the model structure 2. **C++ → Machine code**: The generated C++ is compiled by your local C++ compiler (e.g., `g++` via `Rtools` on Windows) into a **native shared library** (`.so` / `.dll`). This is binary code your CPU can execute directly. The result is a compiled model object in R — essentially a self-contained, highly optimized executable. #### Why This Design? - **Performance**: Native machine code runs orders of magnitude faster than interpreted code. Bayesian sampling requires evaluating the log-posterior and its **gradients thousands to millions of times** — speed is critical. - **Automatic differentiation**: The C++ translation sets up the *autodiff* tape, enabling exact gradient computation (not numerical approximation) needed by HMC/NUTS. #### Relationship to the Sampling Step The two steps have a clean **compile-once, sample-many** relationship: | Step | What happens | Analogy | |------------------------|------------------------|------------------------| | **Compilation** | Translates + optimizes the model into machine code | Building a specialized calculator | | **Sampling** | Runs HMC/NUTS using the compiled code, feeding in your data | Using that calculator repeatedly | ### Sampling (MCMC with HMC/NUTS) There are several conceptual and computation layers in the sampling step. #### Layer 1: **MCMC Iteration Level** (Top Layer) - Each iteration = one proposal → acceptance/rejection decision - You control this with `iter_sampling` (e.g., 1000 iterations) - Each iteration generates **one posterior sample** (after warmup) - Multiple chains run independently → better convergence diagnostics > *Example: 4 chains × 1000 iterations = 4,000 posterior samples* #### Layer 2: **Trajectory Construction** (HMC/NUTS Core) - Within each iteration, Stan builds a **Hamiltonian trajectory** using **leapfrog steps** - NUTS automatically chooses how many steps to take (avoids manual tuning) - Each leapfrog step: - Updates position (parameters: e.g., `pi`) - Updates momentum (auxiliary variable) - Uses gradient of log-posterior > *This is where the “simulation” happens — the sampler explores the parameter space* #### Layer 3: **Gradient Evaluation** (Computational Core) - At each leapfrog step, Stan computes: - **Log-posterior**: `log(p(data | parameters) × p(parameters))` - **Gradient**: ∇ log-posterior (via automatic differentiation) - This is where the **compiled C++ code** runs — fast and exact - The gradient tells the sampler which direction to move for efficient exploration > *This is the “engine” — the reason Stan is so fast and accurate* #### Layer 4: **Model Evaluation** (Lowest Layer) - The compiled model evaluates: - Likelihood: `Y ~ binomial(n_trials, pi)` - Prior: `pi ~ beta(2, 2)` - Generated quantities (if any) - All this is pre-compiled into C++ → runs at machine speed > *This is the “model structure” you defined — now being executed millions of times* #### Sampling summary | Layer | What Happens | Controlled By | Frequency | |-------|--------------|-------------|---------| | 1. MCMC Iteration | One sample per iteration | `iter_sampling` | 1,000–10,000× | | 2. Leapfrog Steps | Trajectory construction | NUTS (automatic) | 10–100× per iteration | | 3. Gradient Eval | Compute log-posterior + gradient | Compiled model | 10–100× per iteration | | 4. Model Eval | Evaluate likelihood + prior | Stan code | 10–100× per iteration | ### Key implications The whole process is also called **simulating the posterior** - An flexible defined model **does not contain data** - The compiled object **knows nothing about your data yet** — Data is passed at sampling time - You can **reuse the compiled model** with different datasets or priors without recompiling - Sampling calls the compiled log-posterior + gradient function **at every leapfrog step** of HMC, which is why having it in fast native code matters so much Compilation is a **one-time translation cost** that makes the repeated, expensive work of sampling as fast as possible. The sampler is essentially a tight loop calling the compiled C++ function millions of times — without compilation, this would be prohibitively slow in interpreted R or Python. ## CmdStanR versus RStan In "Different Software for Bayesian Analysis" @sec-905-software-for-bayesian-analysis I decided to change from RStan {**rstan**} to CmdStanR {**cmdstanr**}. The next step is to transfer the RStan "Beta-Binomial example" @sec-006-beta-binomial-example into CmdRStanR and to compare the two approaches. The model definition written in Stan is by and large in both approaches the same. Nevertheless I found five possible improvements. Here is a detailed comparison of the **modern CmdStanR code** with the **"Bayes Rules!" code**: ### Model definition The model definition written in Stan is by and large in both approaches the same. Nevertheless I found several improvements. #### **Integration approach:** `.stan` file vs. character string The first improvement does not address the content of the model definition but the mode of integration. In contrast to the "Bayes rules!" book which uses a character string within R to describe the model, the recommended approach is to use a separate file with a `.stan` extension. To make the comparison between the book and my version I will show in the first part of the following experiment the code from "Bayes rules!". :::::: my-experiment :::: my-experiment-header ::: {#def-905-stan-file} : Display `.stan` file with model code in Quarto document ::: :::: ::: my-experiment-container There are two options: 1. Using R `base::cat(base::readLines())` function: You need to apply the `#| class-output: stan` chunk option. The following code lines would the `.stan` file include into the Quarto document: ```r #| class-output: stan cat(readLines("include/stan/905-exp-rstan-beta-binomial.stan"), sep = "\n") ``` The final `\n` is necessary, because when a Quarto file is missing a trailing empty line the R parser may issue an "incomplete final line" warning or fail to read the last row correctly, as the parser expects the file to end with a newline character. The above code results in the following code snippet. ::: {.cell} ```{#lst-rstan-beta-binomial .r .cell-code} cat(readLines("include/stan/905-exp-rstan-beta-binomial.stan"), sep = "\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` stan #> // #> // This Stan program defines a Beta-Binomial model, #> // as explained in chapter 6 of "Bayes Rules!" #> #> #> data { #> int Y; #> } #> parameters { #> real pi; #> } #> model { #> Y ~ binomial(10, pi); #> pi ~ beta(2, 2); #> } ``` ::: ::: 2. Using the [include-code-files](https://github.com/quarto-ext/include-code-files) filter extension. This method renders the Stan code with syntax highlighting, treating it as a Stan code block. It supports other features too, like line numbers, or not inserting the whole file, but a range of lines. (This time I refer to the file with the improved version) ```` ``` {.stan include="include/stan/905-exp-cmdstanr-beta-binomial.stan" code-line-numbers="true"} ``` ```` The above code results in the following code snippet: ```{.stan include="include/stan/905-exp-cmdstanr-beta-binomial.stan" code-line-numbers="true"} ``` ::: :::::: #### **Side-by-Side Comparison:** CmdStanR vs. RStan | Aspect | Modern Code (CmdStanR) | "Bayes Rules!" Code | |--------|------------------------|-------------------| | **Data block structure** | Parameterized with `n`, `n_trials` | Hardcoded with `upper = 10` | | **Array syntax** | `array[n] int Y` | `int Y` | | **Flexibility** | Reusable for any number of trials | Fixed for 10 trials only | | **Likelihood** | `Y ~ binomial(n_trials, pi)` | `Y ~ binomial(10, pi)` | | **Prior/Likelihood order** | Prior first, then likelihood | Likelihood first, then prior | | **Spaces in syntax** | No spaces around `=` and `<` | Spaces around `=` and `<` | #### **Data Block:** Flexibility vs. Simplicity **Modern Code:** ```stan data { int n; // number of observations int n_trials; // number of trials array[n] int Y; } ``` **"Bayes Rules!" Code:** ```stan data { int Y; } ``` **Difference:** - Modern code is **parameterized** — you can pass `n_trials` as data, making the model reusable. - "Bayes Rules!" is **hardcoded** — the number of trials (10) is fixed in the model definition. - Modern code declares `n` (number of observations) for potential multiple observations. #### **Array Syntax:** Modern vs. Legacy **Modern Code:** ```stan array[n] int Y; ``` **"Bayes Rules!" Code:** ```stan int Y; ``` **Difference:** - Modern uses **`array[n]` syntax** (Stan 2.26+) — more intuitive, size comes first. - "Bayes Rules!" uses **scalar declaration** — only one observation `Y`. - Modern code scales to multiple observations; "Bayes Rules!" is single-observation only. #### **Model order:** Prior first, then Likelihood **Modern Code:** ```stan model { // Prior pi ~ beta(2, 2); // Likelihood Y ~ binomial(n_trials, pi); } ``` **"Bayes Rules!" Code:** ```stan model { Y ~ binomial(10, pi); pi ~ beta(2, 2); } ``` **Difference:** - Modern code lists **prior first, then likelihood** (pedagogically clearer for Bayesian thinking). - "Bayes Rules!" lists **likelihood first, then prior** (mathematically equivalent, but less intuitive). - **Functionally identical** — Stan doesn't care about order. #### **Spacing Convention:** No spaces around operators **Modern Code:** ```stan int Y; ``` **"Bayes Rules!" Code:** ```stan int Y; ``` **Difference:** - Modern code uses **no spaces** around `=` and `<` (modern Stan style). - "Bayes Rules!" uses **spaces** (older style, still valid). - **Functionally identical** — both are valid syntax. #### **Processing:** Separate steps vs. combined call **Modern Code uses CmdStanR:** ```r model <- cmdstan_model("model.stan") fit <- model$sample(data = data_list, chains = 4, ...) ``` **"Bayes Rules!" likely uses RStan:** ```r fit <- stan(file = "model.stan", data = data_list, chains = 4, ...) ``` **Difference:** - **CmdStanR** — separate compilation and sampling steps: more explicit, and faster. - **RStan** — combined in one `rstan::stan()` call: simpler, but less transparent. (But one could in Rstan also separate compilation and sampling with `rstan::stan_model()` and `rstan::sampling()`.) #### **Summary Table:** CmdStanR vs. RStan | Feature | Modern Code | "Bayes Rules!" | |---------|------------|----------------| | **Generalizability** | ✅ Reusable for any `n_trials` | ❌ Fixed to 10 trials | | **Multiple observations** | ✅ Supports `n > 1` | ❌ Single observation only | | **Stan version** | ✅ Modern (2.26+) | ✅ Works in all versions | | **Readability** | ✅ Clear prior/likelihood structure | ✅ Simple and concise | | **Production use** | ✅ Flexible and scalable | ❌ Limited to specific case | ::: {.callout-important #imp-905-lesson-learned-model-definition} ###### Model definition: Lesson learned - **For learning** (like "Bayes Rules!") — The simple version is fine; it's easier to understand. - **For research/production** — Use the modern, parameterized version for flexibility and reusability. - **Best practice** — Always parameterize fixed values like `n_trials` so your model generalizes. ::: ## Compilation Caching with CmdStanR It was important for my understanding to separate compilation and sampling. Beside of the conceptual reason separating compilation from sampling has another advantage: You can cache the compiled model and run it many times with different data without repeating the time-consuming compilation step. ### Why This Matters | Aspect | CmdStanR | rstan | |--------|----------|-------| | **Compilation** | Once per session | Every `stan()` call | | **Time saved** | Significant (especially for complex models) | None | | **Efficiency** | ✅ Excellent for multiple analyses | ❌ Wasteful | | **Use case** | Fitting same model to different data | Single fit | For instance I could run my Beta-Binomial example model with a different number of trials. See as an example the following pseudocode: ```r ## Pseudocode Snippet library(cmdstanr) # Compile once model <- cmdstan_model("model.stan") # Fit to different datasets without recompilation fit_10_trials <- model$sample(data = list(n = 1, n_trials = 10, Y = array(9)), ...) fit_20_trials <- model$sample(data = list(n = 1, n_trials = 20, Y = array(18)), ...) fit_100_trials <- model$sample(data = list(n = 1, n_trials = 100, Y = array(90)), ...) ``` **All three fits use the same compiled model** — this arrangement is a huge time saver! ### Default Behavior (Without Explicit Caching) **By default, re-knitting a Quarto document will recompile the model** because: - Each code chunk runs in a fresh R session (or at least a new environment). - The `model` object from `cmdstan_model()` is not automatically persisted between knits. ```r ## Pseudocode Snippet # This gets re-run every time you knit model <- cmdstan_model("model.stan") # ← Recompiles each time! It communicates with Stan through the command-line interface (**CmdStan**) rather than interfacing directly with C++ via `Rcpp`. It’s ideal if you prefer **modular workflows** where Stan handles computation and downstream R packages (like `posterior` or `bayesplot`) handle analysis {**cmdstanr**} offers several advantages: - **Always up-to-date**: Automatically stays compatible with the latest Stan releases. - **Fewer installation issues**: Avoids common C++ linking and compilation errors associated with RStan. - **More stable**: Reduces unexpected crashes in RStudio. - **Permissive license**: Uses a flexible **BSD-3-Clause license**. **CmdStanR** is generally recommended for new projects due to its active maintenance and lower memory overhead ::: {#imp-905-cmdstanr-reference .callout-important} ###### Learning Bayesian statistics: {rstan} vs {cmdstanr} The book uses the `RStan` interface but the more modern approach is the `CmdStanR` interface. ::: ### Caching Results To understanding caching when using {**rstan**} or {**cmdstanr**} it is important to separate two processes that are combined in the `rstan::stan()` function **1. Compilation of the model**: - `rstan::stan_model(file = )` compiles the Stan model (from file or code) into a stanmodel object. Use this separately when you want to reuse the compiled model across multiple sampling runs (e.g., with different data or initial values). - `my_model <- cmdstanr::cmdstan_model()` is the equivalnet in {**cmdstanr**} **2. Drawing samples** - `rstan::sampling()`: Draws samples from a pre-compiled stanmodel object. Use it after `rstan::stan_model()` when you want to sample without recompiling, enabling faster iteration and model reuse. - `my_model$sample()` is the equivalent in {**cmdstanr**} `rstan::stan()` is high-level function that compiles the model and samples in one step. Use when you want convenience and don’t need to reuse the compiled model. **It automatically checks if recompilation is needed.** **When to use which function in {rstan}?** - Use `rstan::stan()` for quick, one-off analyses. - Use `rstan::stan_model()` + `rstan::sampling()` for modular workflows, especially when fitting the same model to multiple datasets or debugging sampling settings. **When to use {rstan} or {cmdstanr}?** - **Use `rstan`** if you prefer a mature, in-memory interface with extensive documentation and don’t need the latest Stan features immediately. It integrates tightly with R but can be harder to install (especially on Windows) and lags behind Stan releases. - **Use `cmdstanr`** if you want faster access to the latest Stan features, better installation reliability (especially via `install_cmdstan()`), lower memory usage (saves samples to disk), support for within-chain parallelization, and a more permissive BSD license. **It’s now the recommended interface by the Stan team.** > ✅ **Current best practice**: Use `cmdstanr` for new projects unless > you depend on `rstan`-specific workflows. **Option 1: Save/load the fit object with `saveRDS`** *(simplest)* ``` r fit_file <- "my_model_fit.rds" if (file.exists(fit_file)) { fit <- readRDS(fit_file) } else { fit <- stan(file = "model.stan", data = data_list, ...) saveRDS(fit, fit_file) } ``` **Option 2: Cache compiled Stan model separately** Compiling is expensive — cache the compiled model to reuse it: ``` r model_file <- "compiled_model.rds" if (file.exists(model_file)) { model <- readRDS(model_file) } else { model <- stan_model(file = "model.stan") saveRDS(model, model_file) } fit <- sampling(model, data = data_list, ...) ``` **Option 3: Use the `targets` package** *(best for reproducible pipelines)* ``` r # _targets.R library(targets) list( tar_target(stan_data, prepare_data()), tar_target(stan_model, stan_model("model.stan")), tar_target(fit, sampling(stan_model, data = stan_data, ...)) ) ``` `targets` automatically skips re-running steps when inputs haven't changed. ### Quick Summary | Goal | Approach | |-------------------------|------------------------------------------| | Faster sampling | Parallelize chains, tune `iter`/`warmup` | | Better model efficiency | Vectorize, non-centered parameterization | | Cache compiled model | `saveRDS` on `stan_model()` | | Cache full fit | `saveRDS` on the fit object | | Reproducible pipeline | Use `targets` package | :::::::::: my-experiment :::: my-experiment-header ::: {#def-905-exp-cache-full-fit} : Cache the fit object ::: :::: ::::::: my-experiment-container If I want a recompilation of the `stanfit` object, than I have to delete in the following code example the locally stored `.rds` object manually. :::::: my-r-code :::: my-r-code-header ::: {#cnj-905-exp-cache-full-fit} : Cache the full fit with `saveRDS` on the fit object ::: :::: ::: my-r-code-container ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} fit_file <- "my_model_fit.rds" if (file.exists(fit_file)) { fit <- readRDS(fit_file) } else { fit <- stan(file = "model.stan", data = data_list, ...) saveRDS(fit, fit_file) } ``` ::: ::: :::::: ::::::: :::::::::: ## Glossary Entries {.unnumbered} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
Advanced Organizer Advance organizers are pedagogic devices that bridge the gap between what learners already know and what learners need to know. (<a href="https://link.springer.com/referenceworkentry/10.1007/978-1-4419-1428-6_157">Encyclopedia of the Science of Learning</a>)
ADVI ADVI stands for Automatic Differentiation Variational Inference. It is a method for approximating complex Bayesian posterior distributions by transforming the inference problem into an optimization task. ADVI automatically derives variational inference algorithms without requiring conjugacy assumptions, leveraging automatic differentiation to compute gradients and stochastic gradient ascent to optimize the evidence lower bound (ELBO). This enables scalable and automated approximate Bayesian inference across a broad class of probabilistic models.
Beta-Binomial-Model The Beta-Binomial Bayesian Model is a fundamental framework in Bayesian statistics used to estimate a proportion π (e.g., success probability) when data are binary outcomes (success/failure) across n independent trials. The Beta-Binomial Bayesian Model combines a Beta prior with a Binomial likelihood, resulting in a Beta posterior due to conjugacy. This makes it ideal for estimating unknown proportions (e.g., success rates) from binary data.
BFGSx BFGS stands for Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno, named after the four researchers who developed the algorithm.
Brave Leo AI Brave Leo is a privacy-first, browser-integrated AI assistant developed by Brave Software and built directly into the Brave browser for desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux) and mobile (Android, iOS). It allows users to interact with web content—such as summarizing articles, analyzing PDFs and Google Docs, translating text, generating content, and answering questions—without leaving the current tab.
Cache Caching is the process of storing frequently accessed data in a high-speed, temporary storage layer so that future requests for that data can be served faster than accessing the primary storage location. By keeping copies of data in fast hardware like RAM or memory, caching reduces latency, lowers backend load, and improves overall application performance without needing to recompute results or refetch data from slower sources like disks or databases.
Claude Haiku Claude Haiku is Anthropic’s smallest, fastest, and most cost-effective model in the Claude family, designed for high-speed, low-latency tasks while maintaining strong performance on coding, computer use, and agent workflows.
CRAN CRAN stands for the Comprehensive R Archive Network, which is R's central software repository, supported by the R Foundation. It contains an archive of the latest and previous versions of the R distribution, documentation, and contributed R packages. (https://cran.r-project.org/)
DSO A Dynamic Shared Object (DSO) is a type of library file used on Unix-like operating systems (such as Linux and macOS) that contains code and data that can be shared among multiple programs at runtime. When you compile C++ code into a DSO, you're creating a shared library (typically with a .so extension on Linux) that can be dynamically loaded by an executable during execution, enabling code reuse, reduced memory usage, and easier updates without recompiling the main program
GitHub GitHub is a web-based platform that allows developers to create, store, manage, and share their code. It uses Git, a distributed version control system, to track changes in code and facilitate collaboration among developers. GitHub provides a user-friendly interface that makes it easier for individuals and teams to use Git for version control and collaboration. GitHub is commonly used to host open-source software development projects.
Gradient In the context of R Bayesian analysis, the term gradient typically refers to the rate of change of a function, often used in optimization or inference processes. In a Bayesian context the gradient helps to navigate efficiently through the parameter space without having to directly calculate the full posterior.
L-BFGS L-BFGS (Limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno) is a quasi-Newton optimization algorithm used to solve large-scale unconstrained optimization problems. It is a memory-efficient variant of the BFGS algorithm, designed for problems with a very large number of variables (e.g., >1000), where storing the full Hessian matrix is impractical.
LLMs Large Language Models (LLMs) are advanced artificial intelligence systems trained on massive amounts of text data to understand, generate, and manipulate human language. LLMs function as statistical prediction machines, learning patterns in language by predicting the next word in a sequence. This allows them to perform diverse tasks such as answering questions, writing essays, translating languages, summarizing documents, generating code, and even engaging in conversation. (Brave-AI)
MCMC Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods comprise a class of algorithms for sampling from a probability distribution. By constructing a [markov chain] that has the desired distribution as its equilibrium distribution, one can obtain a sample of the desired distribution by recording states from the chain. The more steps that are included, the more closely the distribution of the sample matches the actual desired distribution. Various algorithms exist for constructing chains. (<a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markov_chain_Monte_Carlo">Wikipedia</a>)
NUTS The abbreviation "NUTS" stands for **No U-Turn Sampler** and is a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) Method. This means that it is not a Markov Chain method and thus, this algorithm avoids the random walk part, which is often deemed as inefficient and slow to converge. Instead of doing the random walk, NUTS does jumps of length x. Each jump doubles as the algorithm continues to run. This happens until the trajectory reaches a point where it wants to return to the starting point. ([CrossValidated](https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/311813/can-somebody-explain-to-me-nuts-in-english)) (Chap.4 in my notes)
Positron Assistant Positron Assistant is an AI coding assistant built specifically for data science workflows within the Positron IDE, designed to enhance R and Python development. It provides chat support, inline assistance, and code completions with deep context from your interactive data science work, including loaded data, plots, and console history.
Pseudocode Pseudocode is an informal, high-level description of a computer program or algorithm written in plain English mixed with programming-like structures, rather than a formal programming language. It serves as a syntax-free blueprint that outlines the logic and steps of a process without adhering to the strict rules or syntax of any specific coding language. Unlike actual code, pseudocode cannot be compiled or executed by a computer; it is designed exclusively for human understanding to help developers plan, design, and communicate algorithms before implementation.
Stan Platform Stan is a state-of-the-art platform for statistical modeling and high-performance statistical computation. Stan interfaces with the most popular data analysis languages (R, Python, shell, MATLAB, Julia, Stata) and runs on all major platforms (Linux, Mac, Windows). Users specify log density functions in Stan’s probabilistic programming language and get (a) full Bayesian statistical inference with MCMC sampling (NUTS, HMC), (b) approximate Bayesian inference with variational inference (ADVI), (c) penalized maximum likelihood estimation with optimization (L-BFGS). Stan is named in honor of Stanislaw Ulam (1909-1984), co-inventor of the Monte Carlo method. (<a href="https://mc-stan.org/">STAN website</a> and <a href="https://www.r-bloggers.com/2019/01/an-introduction-to-stan-with-r/">R-Bloggers</a>)
